title: Sparse attention integration for long-document workloads — Arch review notes
summary: Review of proposed integration of sparse-attention kernels to support long-context (8k-1M tokens) generation workloads. Focus: runtime kernel selection, KV cache compatibility, memory/latency tradeoffs, interaction with quantized paths, and safe rollout strategy across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments.
discussion_points: Motivation: several customers and internal benchmarks show quadratic attention dominates cost for >16k tokens; sparse approaches (block sparse, local+global, BigBird-like masks) reduce compute but change kernel shapes and KV semantics.
Kernel availability: upstream kernel prototypes exist for NVIDIA Ampere/Blackwell and for certain CPU sparse libs; currently no uniform CUDA/cuBLAS-compatible sparse kernel in our runtime.
KV cache model mapping: sparse attention implies different key/value storage patterns (block-indexed vs contiguous), challenging current KV prefix caching layer and eviction heuristics.
Quantization interactions: many sparse approaches rely on block/row formats that don't map cleanly to quantized int8 kernels; need fallbacks or dequantize/compute paths.
Fallback and graceful degradation: proposal for hybrid mode — try sparse kernel when sequence length and model flags match, otherwise fallback to dense kernel variant.
Performance goals and SLOs: target p50 token latency within 1.2x of dense for 32k sequences and p99 within 1.5x while reducing memory by 2x in common long-doc workloads.
Safety for Private deployments: binary/kernel shipping constraints and signed artifacts; customers may restrict kernel installs — must support a dense-only fallback.
Testing & eval plan: synthetic long-context benchmarks, real-customer prompt corpus, quality regression checks on perplexity/LL and end-to-end user-facing metrics.
Migration path for models: model-side changes minimal, prefer adapter layers or model-variant tagging instead of requiring new model formats.
Observability: need new telemetry (sparse-kernel-used bool, fragmentation-metrics, cache-miss-patterns) and dashboards for rollout monitoring.
Cost accounting: metric to attribute token-cost savings and GPU-hrs delta for customers using sparse mode; impact on billing not decided yet.
Security and determinism: sparse kernels introduce non-determinism across hardware types; must document and provide opt-out flags for reproducibility-sensitive workloads.
alternatives_considered: Do nothing: keep dense-only path. Pros: simplest, widest compatibility. Cons: high cost for long contexts, customer churn risk.

Model-side truncation + retrieval: avoid long contexts by moving to retrieval augmentation. Pros: immediate ROI for some apps. Cons: changes app UX and not always applicable for single-document generation.
Server-side chunking with stitched generation: split long documents into chunks, synthesize. Pros: requires no new kernels. Cons: quality regressions and complex reranking/state management.
Adopt third-party runtime with built-in sparse kernels. Pros: quicker integration. Cons: vendor lock-in, mismatch with existing telemetry and rollout tooling.
decisions: Proceed with a hybrid sparse-dense strategy: implement sparse kernels behind a runtime feature flag and use a deterministic kernel-selection policy based on sequence length, model annotation, and hardware capability.
Maintain KV cache compatibility by introducing a thin adapter layer in KV-store that can present a contiguous interface to upper layers while storing sparse-friendly blocks internally.
Keep quantized paths: provide dequantize->sparse->requantize paths initially for correctness, optimize later for int8 sparse kernels when upstream support matures.
Require signed kernel artifacts for Private deployments. If customer-managed kernels are not present, runtime will force dense fallback and log telemetry for guidance.
Add telemetry flags: sparse_kernel_used, sparse_fragmentation, kv_adapter_evictions to runtime traces and expose per-customer dashboards during rollout.
Create a gated rollout: start with internal canaries, then opt-in beta for Dedicated customers, then staged rollout for Hosted with kill-switch and A/B quality checks.
tradeoffs: Latency vs memory: sparse reduces memory footprint but may increase token latency due to more complex kernel indexing and cache adapters.
Complexity vs benefit: introduces significant runtime complexity, more testing surface, but large cost savings for long-context customers.
Compatibility vs performance: keeping dense fallback increases compatibility but means some customers won't see benefits unless fully on-boarded.
risks: Quality regressions: sparse attention patterns could change attention distribution and degrade downstream task quality — need prompt-level regression tests.
Operational fragility: new kernels may have platform-specific bugs causing crashes — must have immediate fallbacks and rapid rollback playbooks.
Billing ambiguity: savings need to be translated into customer-visible price signals or credits; otherwise finance concerns may arise.
Private deployment constraints: customers who cannot install kernels may be unaware they are not getting sparse benefits — need clear messaging.
